about: Accrue brand data, version 2.1. Every rule in the brand book as structured data; American English.
name: Accrue

revisions.changes: The logo sound is a quiet, close felt-tip recording, drawn with a steady ruled stroke; the confirm sound follows it, at a lower cue level. Color names open on a tap on phones, every page carries the browser-tab icon, and the invoice total on the idea page lines up on phones.

A new identity: the lowercase Besley wordmark with a bookkeeper’s double line under it, the ledger palette with its paid and pending colors, Besley, Public Sans and IBM Plex Mono, voice, motion, sound, imagery, the brand’s place inside host applications and the files to use it all.

idea.line: Accrue puts the double line of a final total under its name.
explanation: On invoices, statements and spreadsheets, a double line under a number means it is the final total. Nothing below it changes.

Accrue’s job is to know which charges, refunds and invoices are final. A refund you requested is not final; a refund Stripe has confirmed is. So the logo puts that double line under the name. In the docs, in Accrue Admin and on invoices, the same line marks what is final. No other billing or payments brand uses it.

positioning: Open-source billing for Phoenix apps, kept in your own database. Nothing shows as paid until Stripe or Braintree says it is.
job: Give my Phoenix app billing I can trust, and let me see exactly what is known and what is still pending.

audience.job: When I add billing to my Phoenix app, I want subscriptions and payments in my own database, so my app always knows which customers have paid.
audience.needs: Billing that fits a normal Phoenix app, setup in a few Mix commands, and a way to test the whole flow without real payments.

audience.job: When I compare billing libraries, I want one that’s easy to start with and safe to depend on for years, so I can commit to it with confidence.
audience.needs: Easy setup, a realistic demo, flexibility for how they bill, and signs of a healthy open-source project.

audience.job: When a customer asks about a charge, I want to see what happened to it, so I can answer without asking an engineer.
audience.needs: One place in Accrue Admin to look up a customer, see their plan and what they owe, and fix the problem.

audience.job: When I go to pay my invoice, I want it to look like the company I signed up with, so I know it’s genuine.
audience.needs: The company’s own brand on every email, invoice and billing page, with no mention of Accrue.

values.meaning: Say what Accrue does (“verifies every webhook signature”), not how great it is (“bank-grade”).
Use the real names: the actual module, the actual version, `Accrue.Billing.subscribe/3` rather than “the API”.
Speak Elixir: Ecto schemas, contexts, plugs and Mix tasks, used the way Phoenix developers use them.
Pending is not paid. When Accrue doesn’t know, it says so instead of guessing.
Words and design that still hold up in five years: no trends, no dated slang.

rules: The name is never shown without its double line.
Green means paid, brass means pending, always with the status word.
Say what it does, not how good it is.

presence.head: Accrue lives inside the apps that use it. The brand knows when to be quiet.

logo.wordmark: accrue, lowercase, in Besley SemiBold (weight 600) with no extra letter spacing, converted to outlines (drawn shapes, not live text). It is a drawing: never typed in the font.
logo.rule: The double line is drawn from the letters: each bar is 100 font units thick (the font’s em is 2,000), the weight of Besley’s thinnest horizontal stroke (the top of the a’s bowl), so it reads as part of the type and not as an underline. The bars are 68 units apart and the first sits 120 units under the baseline; “accrue” has no descenders, so the line can sit close. It runs exactly from the a’s left edge to the e’s right edge.
logo.together: The word and the line are one logo. The line is never shown alone as the logo, and the word is never shown without it.
logo.mono: In one-color versions, the word and the line use the same color. They are separate pieces that never touch, so the line never has to break around a letter.
logo.symbol: The symbol is the a alone, with its own double line under it, as wide as the a. It is drawn for each size rather than scaled: at 16, 24, 32, 48 and 64 px the x-height, the baseline, the a’s stem and both lines sit on whole pixels, the a gets a little heavier as it gets smaller (weight 640 at 64 px, 700 at 16), and each line is the a’s thin stroke at that size, rounded to whole pixels.
logo.icon: The app tile is the symbol on Ledger Green: a Ledger Paper “a” over a double line in Mint Line. Each size has its own drawing, so even the 16 px favicon keeps two distinct 1-pixel lines: they blur only when a large drawing is scaled down, so we never scale one down.
logo.iconMore: We supply square files. GitHub, Hex and social sites crop avatars to circles and rounded squares themselves; the symbol is centered with room for their crop. Never draw the symbol inside a circle yourself.
logo.wordAlone: Where a logo can’t be placed, write Accrue as plain text.
logo.clear: Keep one x-height (the height of a lowercase x in the wordmark) of clear space on every side of the lockup: no text, page edges or other logos inside it. The line counts as part of the logo.
logo.minNote: Below 96 px wide each line would be thinner than 1.4 pixels and the two would start to merge; use the symbol instead. Below 64 px always use the symbol file drawn for that size. Print sizes assume offset or good digital printing; check engraving and embroidery with the supplier.
misuse: Don’t use the word without the line.
Don’t make the line a single line or blue: it reads as a link.
Don’t put the line through or above the word.
Don’t stretch, slant or outline it.
Don’t lock a tagline to it.
Don’t put it in a box or badge.
Don’t set it on Line Green or coral.

status.meaning: Done, in Stripe’s or Braintree’s own words: paid, refunded, active. Shown with the Paid mark, a small double line, beside the word. Paid Ink on light, Mint Line on dark.
A charge or refund sent to Stripe or Braintree that they haven’t confirmed yet, or a webhook received and not yet applied. Brass Ink on light, Brass on dark.
Refused or failed, by Stripe, Braintree or Accrue. Red Ink on light, a lighter red on dark. Bookkeepers’ red, used sparingly.
Stripe hasn’t sent anything yet, or its last update is old. Pencil on light, Sage on dark, never green or red, because Accrue doesn’t guess.

type.product: Accrue Admin uses Public Sans for its interface and IBM Plex Mono for amounts and IDs; titles in Besley. Customer-facing templates (emails, invoice PDFs) use the host app’s own fonts, from its branding settings (`config :accrue, :branding`).
type.license: All three are under the SIL Open Font License 1.1: free for docs, the web, slides, print and merch. The fonts are in assets/fonts.
type.why: Besley is a revival of the Clarendon that Robert Besley’s foundry registered in 1845: the bracketed slab serif of ledgers, receipts, tickets and printed forms. It carries the feeling of kept records without nostalgia, and no billing library, payment brand or Elixir project is set in it. Public Sans, the open typeface of the U.S. Web Design System, does the reading and the interface without a voice of its own. IBM Plex Mono sets code, identifiers and every figure that has to line up in a column.

writingFor: Write for support staff who don’t read code. Name the customer, the invoice or plan, and the next step; keep the module name and the ID for the engineer.
Never blame the paying customer. “The card was declined”, never “You failed to pay”.
Say who acted. Stripe, Braintree, Accrue or your app: each is a different actor, and the sentence names the right one.

Give amounts their currency and period. In Accrue Admin and the docs, “USD 588.00 per month”, never a bare 588. Customer-facing templates (Portal, invoices, emails) format money in the host app’s own locale and style, such as “$588.00/month”.
Leave out “just”, “simply” and “easy”. Integration has real steps; name them.
Use “they” for a person you don’t know.

name.rule: Accrue in running text, with a capital A. In code, packages and commands: accrue, accrue_admin, accrue_portal. The logo is lowercase; the name in a sentence is not.

never.why: except as a label in capitals

name.more: Accrue ships two interfaces of its own: Accrue Admin, for the host app’s team, and Accrue Portal, where the host app’s customers manage their billing. Customers never see these names. Neither has a logo of its own: Accrue Admin’s header shows the Accrue lockup alone, or the host app’s brand when it white-labels Admin. Possessive: Accrue’s.

words.means: The billing records Accrue keeps in your app’s database.
words.why: Name the thing itself: “the invoice failed”, not “billing state changed”.

words.means: The service that moves the money: Stripe or Braintree.
words.why: The industry’s term. When you mean a specific one, name it: “Stripe sent a webhook”, not “the payment processor sent a webhook”.

words.means: Pending: Accrue has sent a charge or refund and is waiting for the payment processor to confirm it. Paid, refunded or active: the processor has confirmed it.
words.why: These are the status words Stripe and Braintree use, so Accrue’s screens match what people see in those dashboards.

words.means: One message from Stripe or Braintree to your app about something that happened.
words.why: It’s what Accrue’s code and Accrue Admin call these messages.

words.means: Accrue’s built-in stand-in for Stripe, for tests and demos; no money actually moves. `Accrue.Processor.Fake` in code.
words.why: The name says what it’s for: “the test payment processor”, not “the Fake”.

words.means: `MyApp.Billing`, the module Accrue generates in your app; your code calls it.
The Phoenix app that uses Accrue.

voice.wordsNote: These are only the terms the brand depends on; Accrue’s docs own the full glossary. Never write seamless, robust, powerful, bank-grade, production-grade, batteries-included, best-in-class or modern alternative. Say what Accrue does instead.

motion.trackFormat: [ms, value, cubic-bezier easing into this key]; rule1 and rule2 are the drawn length (0 to 1) from the a’s left edge; wordOpacity 0 to 1

keyframes.picture: The word fades in, without moving
The first line is drawn from the a’s left edge: a quick start, a steady speed, a quick stop at the e
A beat, then the second line, shorter in time and drawn the same way
keyframes.sound: a second stroke, shorter, the same level

craft.how: Each line starts quickly, moves at a steady speed and stops quickly at its end, like a pen pulled along a ruler.
The second line is shorter in time than the first: the hand already knows the length.
A 110 ms beat between the lines, so they read as two strokes, not one thick one.
The word is readable before the pen moves, and never moves itself.

movements.name: Close
movements.description: Once, when the logo first appears in a video, a talk or the website: the word, then the two lines drawn left to right. It is the only drawn motion in the brand.

movements.name: Confirm
movements.description: In the docs and in Accrue Admin, the Paid mark draws in beside the word in 200 ms when a value becomes paid, refunded or active: for example, after someone clicks Retry payment and Stripe’s webhook turns the invoice from Pending to Paid. Pending has no mark that moves; nothing pulses while waiting.

movements.name: Reveal
movements.description: Panels and rows appear with an opacity fade of 150 ms or less. Nothing slides in from the side.

motion.never: The line never wipes away, bounces, loops, overshoots the e or draws right to left; the word never moves. Amounts never count up or down. Pending states never pulse or spin. Reduced motion: the finished logo fades in, and the Paid mark appears without drawing.

close.description: Close: two felt-tip strokes drawing the double line, one pen-down per line, the second shorter. Nothing at the end: the logo is simply there.

confirm.description: Confirm: one short felt-tip stroke as a value becomes paid, for videos and talk demos.

rules.rule: Close plays with the logo animation, and on the website only after a click.
plays in videos and live talk demos when a value becomes paid.
always silent. The Paid mark still draws, with no sound. Support teams work in shared offices and on calls, inside the host app.
for errors, never on page load, never in emails.

sound.character: Pen and paper. A felt-tip drawing a steady line: quiet, close and low, one pen-down per line, the level steady rather than swelling, gone the moment the pen lifts; then a second, shorter line. No chime, no tap, no success sound: the line itself is the confirmation. Quiet enough that it never startles anyone while they’re working.

listeningMaster.cueNote: The logo sounds are cues: their master sits 12 dB below the general listening master, because a 0.5 s cue should sit far below speech and music.

source.title: “writing with feltpen”
source.author: stephan
source.license: Public domain, as claimed by PDSounds and shown on Wikimedia Commons
source.done: Two short runs of friction were cut from the recording, slowed to about 1.6 times their length, shaped to the ruled strokes, layered with a soft pen-down and a quiet desk tone, passed through a gentle compressor and the book’s small dry room, then mastered.
source.credit: Sound source: “writing with feltpen” by stephan (2007), via PDSounds and Wikimedia Commons. Its public-domain status rests on the PDSounds claim as shown on Wikimedia Commons. Edited here: stretched, layered and mastered.

sound.sync: Sound and picture share one timeline. Each stroke sits on its line: it starts as the line starts and stops where the line ends, at a steady level while the line moves at a steady speed. The sound is scheduled first and the animation starts when it is heard, so speaker and Bluetooth delay never pull them apart; a stroke may land a touch late, never early.
sound.syncSource: Audio–video sync tolerances: Recommendation ITU-R BT.1359-1 (1998), detectability about +45 ms (sound early) to −125 ms (sound late).

messaging.tagline: “Paid means paid.” leads where a reader is already on the page (the README, a talk, the website). Where a string is search-indexed or seen out of context (the GitHub description, Hex.pm, the social card), the descriptor leads and the tagline follows. It is never attached to the logo.
messaging.pitch: Accrue is an open-source billing library for Elixir and Phoenix. It handles subscriptions, invoices, payments and webhooks inside your app, and comes with a ready-made admin dashboard.
pillars: Every verified webhook from Stripe or Braintree becomes a record in your own database.
A charge sent to Stripe isn’t a payment yet. Accrue shows Pending until Stripe confirms it, and only then Paid.
Create a subscription with the test payment processor, send a signed webhook, see it in Accrue Admin, then run `mix verify`.
boilerplate: The Elixir billing library for Phoenix apps.
Accrue is an open-source billing library for Elixir and Phoenix: subscriptions, invoices, payments, recovery and webhooks, kept in your own database.

Accrue is an open-source billing library for Elixir and Phoenix. Your app keeps its own billing module, routes and auth; Accrue handles the rest: subscriptions, invoices and payments as Ecto schemas, signature-verified webhooks, a full event history, a ready-made admin dashboard and a white-labeled customer portal.

Accrue is an open-source billing library for Elixir and Phoenix. It keeps subscriptions, invoices, payments, refunds and each customer’s feature access (their entitlements) in your app’s own database, matching what Stripe or Braintree says. Your app keeps its own billing module (`MyApp.Billing`), routes, auth and config. Every webhook is signature-verified and stored, so you never lose a billing event and can always see how an invoice got to where it is. Your team gets a ready-made billing dashboard, and your customers get a billing portal white-labeled with your brand. MIT licensed.

product.head: Show the product: real code and Accrue Admin.
do: Show real code that works with the current release (`{:accrue, "~> 1.7.0"}`), never pseudo-code.
Take every Accrue Admin screenshot from the demo app with the test payment processor, so each release can retake the same pictures.
Invented customers with plain, obviously fictional names (Acme Bakery, Riverside Dental) and invented amounts. Never a real customer, card or email address.
Light and dark versions of each, at 2× resolution, never upscaled.
dont: No growth dashboards or tilted, glowing screens.
No mock-ups of features that don’t exist, and no claim that Braintree works exactly like Stripe unless it has been tested.
No tilted devices, glowing code or terminal art.
No dashboards of revenue going up: Accrue shows what happened to each payment, not growth.

photo: Daylight and real surfaces: paper, desks, notebooks. Hands rather than faces.
Calm frames with room for a headline beside them.
Muted, natural color, so Ledger Green stays the strongest color on the page.

Diagrams: boxes and arrows in Ledger Green and Column Line on Ledger Paper, with Line Green on the one path that matters. Labels are in Public Sans, module names in IBM Plex Mono.

Icons: the host app’s or the platform’s own set in Accrue Admin; none on Accrue’s own pages.
illustrationDont: Isometric servers, coins flowing through pipes, glowing data streams: generic infrastructure art.
The Elixir drop or the Phoenix bird recolored as Accrue’s: they belong to those projects.
A mascot or a character holding money: the consumer-app world.
frames: A hand with a pen marking a printed sheet; hand only
An ordinary desk with a laptop, nothing legible on screen; no people, no logos

rules.rule: neutral to a touch warm, so whites sit near Ledger Paper, never blue.
gentle. Bright areas stay soft and dark areas never go fully black, so no detail is lost.

treatment.never: No heavy filters, vignettes, fake grain or sepia, and never a teal-and-orange grade. The set should look like it was shot on one quiet afternoon.
treatment.howToApply: A LUT (color lookup table) is a small file that applies one color grade to any photograph. Apply `accrue-ledger-daylight.cube` in Lightroom or Photoshop (Color Lookup), Resolve, Final Cut, Premiere or ffmpeg (`lut3d`), at 100% on a correctly exposed photograph; lower the opacity if a photo was already muted.

graphicDevice.head: The closing line.
text: The brand’s graphic device is the double line itself, taken from the logo: under a page title, under a total, under the headline of a talk slide. It says “this is final” in the convention every ledger has used.

Use it once per surface, as wide as what it sits under, in Line Green on light or Mint Line on dark. In the product, a small double line beside the word marks Paid; the full line goes under totals only.
graphicDevice.never: Not through or above words, not as a section divider, not in blue, not on a pending or failed value, and animated only as one left-to-right draw.

graphicElements.head: A small set of graphic elements, each with one job.
items: The double line under the one final thing on a surface: a title, a total, a slide headline.
Once per surface, as wide as what it sits under.
Amounts and IDs in IBM Plex Mono, right-aligned, with the currency code, so figures line up from top to bottom.
Real figures, or ones clearly marked as samples.
Rows divided by Column Line hairlines, labels in spaced capitals. No zebra stripes, no boxes.
Use it for data to compare, never for page layout.
One sentence in Besley italic, the way a careful person would say it.
Once per surface, on Accrue’s own pages.
graphicElements.never: Not among the graphic elements: coins, piggy banks, wallets, credit cards, stairs and rising arrows, padlocks and shields, dollar signs as decoration, gradients, lined-paper patterns and repeated lines as texture.

inTheProduct.head: In the product: Accrue Admin stays in the background.
inTheProduct.intro: Accrue Admin runs inside the host app. By default it shows Accrue’s own look; a host app can white-label it with its own name, logo and accent. These are starting points for Accrue Admin’s theme, not component specs.
items: Paid in green with its double-line mark, Pending in brass, Failed in red ink. Always show the word: color is never the only signal.
Never green for a charge that has only been sent. Pending is not paid.
Buttons and the selected nav item use Ledger Green (Mint Line on dark), or the host app’s accent if set (`:admin_branding`). Other greens stay on status and the line.
IBM Plex Mono, right-aligned, currency code first, with the double line under the total.
Stripe and Braintree IDs and webhook event IDs in IBM Plex Mono, on Folio, selectable.
Never truncate an ID without a way to copy it whole.
inTheProduct.shape: Shape: small, soft corners (a 6 px radius), flat surfaces and hairlines instead of shadows. These are Accrue’s own values for radius and elevation; a host app can override them in Accrue Admin’s theme. The header shows one name, never two: Accrue with “Admin”, or the host app’s own once white-labeled.

messagePattern: What happened, in the past tense, naming the object.
What is pending, and who acts next: Stripe, Braintree, Accrue, the host app or the person reading.
What they can do, as a link or button named for its outcome.

Payment declined by the card issuer. Recovery retries on Nov 3. Retry now or email the customer.
No update: no webhook has arrived for this charge in 24 hours. Check it in the Stripe dashboard.
Cancel Riverside Dental’s Team plan now? Access ends today. No refund is issued.
No invoices match these filters. [[Clear filters]]
messages.notThis: Clear or adjust the filters above to inspect matching billing records.

messageRules: Use the support team’s words: customer, subscription, invoice, payment, refund. Module names and other technical terms belong in the details, for engineers.
Name the action for its result: “Cancel at period end”, “Cancel now”, “Retry payment”, never “Submit” or “OK”. A button or link on its own has no final period.
Before a destructive action, say what it affects and what happens, and offer the safer option beside it.
Say what the system does in the present tense (“updates when the webhook arrives”, not “will update”). No exclamation marks, no “Success”, and no middle dots as separators: use a comma or a new line.

type.spec: IBM Plex Mono 400, 14/20 px, tabular, right-aligned

neutrals.light: Ledger Green, or the host app’s accent if one is set
neutrals.dark: Mint Line, or the host app’s accent if one is set

neutrals.light: a 2 px Ledger Green outline, 2 px off the element

do: On photographs and screenshots, place the lockup on a calm area: a wall, a table top, empty paper.
Use the light lockup over light areas and the dark lockup over dark ones, with the clear space free of detail.
If no calm area exists, move the logo off the image onto Ledger Paper or Ledger Green beside it.
dont: No boxes, badges or blurred panels behind the logo.
Never over code, tables or figures, where the line reads as an underline.

useByOthers: Hex packages, blogs, newsletters and conference sites may use the lockup and symbol unaltered, from these files, at no less than the minimum sizes.
In your own writing, write the name as plain text, “Accrue”; never imitate the wordmark.
Packages that extend Accrue use their own names and marks, and may say “for Accrue”, as in “Tax rates for Accrue”. They don’t use the double line.
Host apps never put the Accrue logo on their customers’ invoices, emails or Portal, and no “Powered by Accrue” line is needed.
Don’t use the marks to suggest an endorsement, audit or partnership that doesn’t exist.
legal: Accrue is not a registered trademark. Use ™ (not ®) only to claim the name as a trademark, once, on the first prominent use in marketing; never on the logo itself.

Not to be confused with the consumer savings app, also named Accrue, at byaccrue.com: it is a different company. Accrue the library never uses wallet, savings or rewards language, coral or red as a brand color, or growth imagery.
The code is MIT-licensed. This book asks that the name and logo identify the official project only (see above).
Credit Pay (Ruby) and Laravel Cashier as prior art; never compare Accrue against them.
Fonts: SIL Open Font License 1.1 (see assets/fonts). Trademark clearance has not been done (see To review).
contact: Questions about the brand and requests to use it: the Accrue maintainers, through the project’s GitHub issues (github.com/szTheory/accrue).
Approval: changes to the logo, colors, type or sounds need a maintainer’s approval and a new version of this book. Everyday applications that follow these rules need none.
This book is versioned: touch-ups raise the decimal (2.1), a new identity raises the whole number (3.0). The revision history is below.

notNeeded.why: Considered, not proposed. A billing library is trusted for being exact; a character would pull it toward the consumer-app world it must stay out of.
A repeated double line reads as lined paper or a strikethrough. The double line appears once per surface.
Accrue is a Hex package with no shop, office or stationery. HexDocs and the README are where people find it and where it speaks.

Host apps never show Accrue to their customers, so there is no co-brand lockup. For conference or sponsor pairings, put the partner’s logo to the right with a 1 px Column Line divider, at a matching x-height.

openDecisions.detail: Ledger Green #17392D, Line Green #3F8A68, Mint Line #8FCBAA, Brass #D1A24E and Brass Ink #7D5A1F, as presented.
Added in the book: #A33A2C on light, #F0937F on dark, always with the word; Paid Ink #2E6B4E for Paid on light.
Pencil or Sage, for when Stripe hasn’t sent anything yet or its last update is old: Accrue’s own rule that no news is neither success nor failure.
Each bar is now 100 units, the weight of the top of the a’s bowl, 68 apart and 120 under the baseline (the presentation drew 64, 44 and 110). The thinner line read as an underline.
Separate pixel-fitted drawings at 16, 24, 32, 48 and 64 px, each keeping both lines. The presentation scaled one drawing down.
Added for the voice line and pull quotes; the presentation used it once.
Sound only on Accrue’s own surfaces, and only after a click.

openDecisions.choice: No Accrue name on host surfaces.
openDecisions.detail: No logo or “Powered by” on invoices, emails or Portal. The branding config’s `business_name` default is “Accrue”; the product may want to require it.

Accrue’s own brand by default (the lockup alone in the header, Ledger Green actions). The host app’s name, logo and accent replace it only when white-labeled, never both. Nothing is set beside the logo: “Admin” would add nothing. The product has to build the default and the switch.

openDecisions.choice: The tagline and the voice principles.
openDecisions.detail: “Paid means paid.” replaces June 2026’s “Billing state, modeled clearly.”; the voice principles (measured, exact, native, durable) carry over.
Ledger Paper for docs, the README and Accrue Admin; Ledger Green for the cover, talks, the social card and dark mode.
A 0.6-second close: the word in 120 ms, the lines drawn 100 to 310 and 420 to 600 ms; a 200 ms Paid mark.
Free-licensed stock, graded with the brand LUT, until the project’s own replace them.

openDecisions.choice: No website grid in the book.
openDecisions.detail: A website build guide sets its own grid within the layout principles.

notChecked: Trademark clearance (another company named Accrue, a consumer savings app, exists; on 30 October 2026 its site (coral on white) and those of Pay, Laravel Cashier and Bling showed none with a serif wordmark or bottle green), print color (proof against a physical swatch; no CMYK or Pantone values are given), the sounds on a range of real speakers, a HexDocs stylesheet and Accrue Admin’s theme built from these values, and the icons as Hex, Livebook and GitHub crop them.
